segments.text: > Part of the [Implementation Status](README.md) index. All require linking a network library (libcurl for fetch/HTTP; system sockets for WebSocket). A server-side HTTP listener (`http.listen(port, handler)`) is tracked under [HTTP-SERVER.md](HTTP-SERVER.md) instead — listening for incoming connections has no browser-side Web API equivalent.

caveats: Setting a `body` without an explicit `method` sends it as `POST` (libcurl's `CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS` implies `POST` unless overridden); an explicit `method` always wins over that default
A fetch carrying an `AbortSignal` resolves at completion, not headers ([ADR-00299](../adr/ADR-00299.md))
notes: `init` is any value with some subset of `method: string` / `headers: Map<string,string> \| Headers` / `body: string` fields; a real `Request` object works as the sole argument too, destructured the same way

Non-blocking I/O ([ADR-00050](../adr/ADR-00050.md)): uses libcurl's multi-interface, driven by the same `select()`-based event loop `http.listen` uses, so `await fetch(...)` inside a connection-handler fiber yields — a slow upstream call doesn't stall other connections or timers
Outside any fiber (plain top-level code, no `http.listen`), there's nothing else to overlap with, so it busy-spins the same multi-interface calls to the same effect as a blocking wait
A network-level failure (DNS, connection refused, TLS, timeout) throws; a non-2xx HTTP status still resolves normally (`.ok` distinguishes it), matching real `fetch`

`await fetch(...)` resolves when the response **headers** arrive (as in real JS, [ADR-00299](../adr/ADR-00299.md)); the body is read lazily — `.text()`/`.json()`/`.arrayBuffer()` drive the transfer to completion, `.body` streams it. A signal-carrying fetch still resolves at completion (its abort machinery lives in the full await)

caveats: **These three methods are synchronous** — they return `string`/parsed value/`ArrayBuffer` directly, not the `Promise<string>`/`Promise<any>`/`Promise<ArrayBuffer>` real WHATWG `fetch` returns. Both call styles work: `const body: string = r.text()` and `await r.text()`/`.json()`/`.arrayBuffer()` (awaiting a non-thenable is identity — a harmless no-op — including the type-directed `.json()` projection through the `await`; [ADR-00241](../adr/ADR-00241.md))

`.json()` reuses `JSON.parse`'s machinery, including its full scope: it validates the body (a non-JSON body — e.g. an HTML error page — throws a catchable `SyntaxError`, [ADR-00223](../adr/ADR-00223.md)) and projects nested objects, array/object-array fields, and top-level `T[]` off the parse tree ([ADR-00224](../adr/ADR-00224.md)); only `any`/`unknown` dynamic shapes remain unsupported
`.text()`/`.json()` are plain null-terminated strings: a binary body with an embedded null byte truncates at the first one, by design — use `.arrayBuffer()` for a binary body
`.text()` after consuming `.body` returns `""` instead of the spec's already-disturbed TypeError; `Object.keys`/JSON of a Response expose an internal `__kml_pending` field
notes: Plain object with `status`/`ok` fields plus `text()`/`json()`/`arrayBuffer()` methods; `.body` is a real `ReadableStream<Uint8Array>` fed incrementally from libcurl's write callback with backpressure via curl pause/unpause ([TDD-00097](../tdd/TDD-00097.md) Stage 4, [ADR-00299](../adr/ADR-00299.md)) — on an already-completed transfer it replays the buffered bytes as one chunk
`.arrayBuffer()` ([ADR-00094](../adr/ADR-00094.md)) carries the real byte count and comes back whole regardless of content

Every string in this compiler is a plain null-terminated C string (`.length` is `strlen`-based), so any string value with an embedded `\0` reads as shorter than it actually is; `.text()`/`.json()` keep that behavior by design (JSON/text bodies aren't expected to legitimately contain embedded nulls) — use `.arrayBuffer()` for a binary body (see [BINARY-DATA-TYPED-ARRAYS.md](BINARY-DATA-TYPED-ARRAYS.md))
Real classes, not just `fetch`'s plain-object `init` (which still works unchanged)

`Headers` is a case-insensitive (lowercased-key) wrapper: `get`/`set`/`has`/`delete` behave like `Map<string,string>`'s own (because storage-wise it *is* one), plus `append(name, value)`, which combines with a comma if `name` is already present instead of overwriting

`new Request(url)` / `new Request(url, init)` builds a plain object (`url`/`method`/`headers`/`body`, all readable directly) — `method` defaults to `"GET"`, `headers` to an empty `Headers`, `body` to `null`
Reverses [ADR-00074](../adr/ADR-00074.md)'s original decision to reject these — see [ADR-00130](../adr/ADR-00130.md)
`http.listen`'s own server-side request-object type annotation is `HttpRequest`, not `Request` — freed up by this change (see the ADR for why)

caveats: Client `new WebSocket(url)` supports **`wss://`** (TLS via libssl — same OpenSSL layer as `tls`, [TDD-00039](../tdd/TDD-00039.md) Stage 4/[ADR-00346](../adr/ADR-00346.md)); the handshake is blocking and verifies the cert (SNI on, no `rejectUnauthorized` opt-out). Server-side `wss` (a TLS listener) is not offered — front it with `tls`/a reverse proxy
Neither side supports binary `.send()` (`ArrayBuffer` payloads)
`.close()` on either side doesn't wait for the peer's own echo back before actually closing (a deliberate simplification)

The client's connect + handshake runs *synchronously*, before the constructor returns, so `.onopen`/`.onerror` are deliberately deferred to the first event-loop pass after construction (giving assignment code a chance to run first) rather than fired inline
notes: Both server and client

Server: `http.listen(port, handler, { ws })`'s optional third-argument handler is called once per successfully upgraded connection with a `WSConnection` (`.onmessage`/`.send(data: string)`/`.close()`), coexisting with ordinary HTTP requests on the same listener; a client `ping` gets an automatic `pong` reply with identical payload (RFC 6455 §5.5.2), and both a peer `close` frame and `.close()` itself send a proper Close frame before the connection ends (RFC 6455 §5.5.1)
A failed connect never throws (`.onerror`/`.onclose` fire instead, matching real `WebSocket`)

See [TDD-00039](../tdd/TDD-00039.md) ([ADR-00125](../adr/ADR-00125.md) Stage 0 frame codec/SHA-1, [ADR-00126](../adr/ADR-00126.md) Stage 1 server handshake, [ADR-00127](../adr/ADR-00127.md) Stage 2 ping/pong + close handshake, [ADR-00128](../adr/ADR-00128.md) Stage 3 client)

caveats: A `retry:`-driven reconnect replays the *full* stored `Last-Event-ID`, not a per-listener value
notes:
Server-sent events (SSE) over HTTP — connection plumbing (`readyState`/`close()`), `onmessage`/`onopen`/`onerror`, `addEventListener`/`removeEventListener` for named (`event: name`) records (`data`/`event`/`id`/`retry` field parsing, multi-line `data:` concatenation), `

`/`

`/bare-`` record boundaries, and auto-reconnect (retries after a dropped connection or network-level connect failure, honoring a server-sent `retry:` delay — default 3000ms — and replaying `Last-Event-ID` as a request header) all work

A response that *arrives* with the wrong shape (non-2xx status, or a 2xx with a `Content-Type` that isn't `text/event-stream`) fails permanently instead of retrying, matching the real spec's distinction between a network failure (retryable) and a malformed response (terminal); the `Content-Type` prefix match is case-insensitive, matching HTTP's case-insensitive header semantics ([ADR-00555](../adr/ADR-00555.md))
See [TDD-00038](../tdd/TDD-00038.md)

caveats: Modeled as the real spec's legacy *synchronous* mode: `.send()`/`.send(body)` runs the request to completion before returning, then fires every registered callback once, synchronously — there's no default-async, callback-interleaved mode (this compiler has no re-entrant-into-already-returned-caller callback machinery to support one)

`.open(method, url, async?, user?, password?)` accepts the optional `async` flag: `async === false` is exact (the request is already synchronous); `async === true` also blocks, since there's no main-thread event loop to defer `.onload` onto — a documented narrowing, not a fake async ([ADR-00615](../adr/ADR-00615.md))
The optional `user`/`password` arguments to `.open()` are accepted (and evaluated) but not yet wired to HTTP auth
`.setRequestHeader(name, value)` accumulates headers, but names are **not** lowercased here (unlike `Headers`' own methods) — a separate V1 narrowing
`.readyState` is 0/1/4 only (UNSENT/OPENED/DONE); the real spec's HEADERS_RECEIVED/LOADING have no meaning for a transfer that always runs to completion in one call
`.responseText`/`.response` are identical values — only a text `responseType` is supported; no `responseType` other than the default
`.onreadystatechange`/`.onload`/`.onerror` callbacks are zero-argument (deliberately — a payload-carrying callback isn't representable for this particular type, see [ADR-00131](../adr/ADR-00131.md))
`.abort()` is a best-effort `readyState` reset — there's nothing to actually interrupt once a synchronous `.send()` has returned
`.getAllResponseHeaders()` returns headers in arrival order, not the spec’s lowercase-sorted order ([ADR-00490](../adr/ADR-00490.md))
notes: Not a blocking implementation: `.send()` is built on the exact same non-blocking `__kml_fetch_async` primitive `fetch()` itself uses, so it still yields the current fiber (rather than blocking every other connection) when called from inside an `http.listen` connection handler

A synchronous `.open(method, url, false)` from inside `klain:sync` worker goroutines yields cooperatively per request (via the shared fetch await path), so pooled workers issue genuinely overlapping requests — the primitive behind the `load_test` load-generator example

Supports `.open(method, url, async?, user?, password?)`, `.setRequestHeader(name, value)`, `.send()`/`.send(body)`, `.abort()`, `.readyState`, `.status`, `.responseText`/`.response`, and the zero-argument callbacks
A network-level failure fires `.onerror` (never throws), matching real `XMLHttpRequest`
See [ADR-00131](../adr/ADR-00131.md)
